newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-French industrial production rebounds in Feb.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-French industrial production rebounds in Feb.

text.p: French industrial production rebounded in February, providing a boost to the ruling centre-right coalition fighting for re-election in the country's snap parliamentary ballot.

The official data released on Thursday showing a 1.6 percent jump in industrial output in February spurred hopes of more robust first-quarter gross domestic product growth. But economists said the economy was not yet poised for takeoff -- especially with further fiscal tightening planned to guarantee France a berth in Europe's proposed single currency.

With unemployment at a record 12.8 percent and forecast to rise, "the economy is undoubtedly a negative" for the right in the May/June election announced by President Jacques Chirac on Monday, said Steven Englander of Smith Barney in Paris. "They certainly cannot run on their economic record."

The 1.6 percent rise in industrial production, stripping out construction, was powered by a strong turnaround in the car sector and semi-finished goods and followed a 1.1 percent fall in January. Output was up 1.6 percent on year-on-year.

Industrial production stripping out energy, agri-food and construction -- seen by national statistics institute INSEE as the best guage of output -- rose an even heftier 3.7 percent in February for a 2.2 percent rise on the year. That measure of output fell 1.1 percent in January.
Politicians seized on the data as proof of recovery. "Growth is taking off again," Budget Minister Alain Lamassoure said.

Economists agreed the numbers were encouraging. "The year is starting out better than expected," said Philippe Brossard of ABN Amro. But they warned the data should be treated cautiously. "Industrial production figures can be very erratic," said Jean-Louis Mourier of Louis Dreyfus Finance.
Some economists were worried by the government's announcement on Thursday of a public spending freeze for 1998 in nominal terms, implying a fall in real terms, could dampen growth.
Although the government had pledged not to raise taxes, economists said the freeze sent a negative message to consumers. "It's going to keep the savings rate high," said one.

"There's concern that fiscal policy tightening could cast a chill," said Darren Williams of UBS. "I was projecting 2.6 percent or higher for economic growth in 1998," said another economist. "Now I think it might be 2.6 percent or lower."
The government is officially targeting a minimum 2.3 percent GDP growth in 1997 and 2.8 percent growth in 1998 after 1.3 percent growth in 1996.

With the number of new entrants into France's labour force climbing, economists also saw no immediate significant easing of unemployment. The jobless rate is forecast by the International Monetary Fund to top 13 percent by mid-year.
"France can grow for a year or two at a pretty decent pace without really reducing the jobless rate," said Englander.

The main consolation for the centre-right against the sluggish economic backdrop, economists said, was that economic remedies proposed by the opposition Socialists do not yet appear to have seized the electorate's imagination.

The Socialists have failed to "build strong political momentum in recent months," said Jean-Francois Mercier of Salomon. "Despite the government's low popularity, Socialist Leader (Lionel) Jospin's plans for alternative economic policies have failed to turn into greater support in opinion polls."

The Socialists are advocating a shorter work week without pay cuts, subsidizing the creation of new public and private sector jobs and, crucially, no further austerity measures to ready France for monetary union.
Polls suggest the ruling centre-right will be re-elected with a comfortable, albeit reduced, majority.
